stem: You are first on scene at a car that struck a utility pole. A wire lies across the hood and the driver is awake inside. What should you do?
options: Pull him out through the far door, away from the wire
Stay back and tell him to stay in the car
Reach in through the window to hold his head still
Lift the wire off the hood with a dry branch
explanation: Treat every downed wire as live. A person in the car is usually safer inside until the power company makes the line safe, and you stay well clear. Wood can carry current, and touching the car puts you in the circuit.

stem: How fast and how deep should you compress the chest of an adult in cardiac arrest?
options: 100 to 120 a minute, at least 2 inches
60 to 80 a minute, about 1 inch
Over 140 a minute, at least 3 inches
80 a minute, as deep as you possibly can push
explanation: Push hard and fast: 100 to 120 compressions a minute, at least 2 inches deep but not more than about 2.4 inches, letting the chest come all the way back up between each one.

stem: A patient opens her eyes and groans only when you squeeze her shoulder. Using AVPU, how is she described?
options: Unresponsive
Alert
Responds to verbal
Responds to pain
explanation: She does not respond to your voice but does react to a painful stimulus, so she is P on the AVPU scale. A patient who responds to nothing is U.

stem: As you walk up, a man sits slumped, pale and silent with blood soaking his pant leg. What does your general impression tell you?
options: He should walk to the ambulance with help
He needs a full history before any other care
He looks sick and needs fast action
He looks stable for now
explanation: The general impression is your first look from across the room. Pallor, silence and heavy bleeding say the patient is sick, so you move straight to the life threats.

stem: When should you check your AED and oxygen supply?
options: At the start of every shift
Only when a warning light flashes on it
Once a year at the agency's equipment inspection
Only after a call where you used them
explanation: A daily or start-of-shift check finds a dead battery, expired pads or an empty cylinder before a patient needs them.

stem: Dispatch reports a fall from a ladder and adds that a caller heard shouting and a gunshot before the fall. What is the safest plan?
options: Ask a bystander to check the patient
Enter quickly, since a patient is down and hurt
Stage nearby until police secure the scene
Park at the door with lights off and go straight in
explanation: A report of a gunshot means the scene may not be safe. You stage out of sight and wait for law enforcement to say it is secure. Sending a bystander in only moves the danger to someone else.

stem: The AED says shock advised. What do you do?
options: Check a pulse before shocking
Remove the pads and reapply them
Give two breaths, then shock
Clear everyone, then shock
explanation: Clear everyone from the patient, press the shock button, then start compressions right away for 2 minutes before the AED analyzes again. A pulse check before the shock only delays it.

stem: An unresponsive woman found in bed has no sign of injury. Which maneuver opens her airway?
options: Pulling the tongue forward with gauze
Head tilt-chin lift
Turning the head side to side
Jaw thrust only
explanation: With no suspected neck injury, the head tilt-chin lift lifts the tongue off the back of the throat. The jaw thrust is kept for patients who may have a spine injury.

stem: In a SAMPLE history, what does the L stand for?
options: Level of consciousness
Last oral intake
Location of the patient's pain
Lung sounds
explanation: SAMPLE covers signs and symptoms, allergies, medications, pertinent past history, last oral intake and events leading up. The last meal matters if surgery or vomiting is likely.

stem: An awake man has blood spurting from a deep cut on his upper arm. What comes first?
options: Take his blood pressure
Control the bleeding
Count his breathing rate
Ask about his allergies
explanation: Massive bleeding can kill in minutes, so it is controlled as soon as you see it, even before a full airway and breathing check in an awake, talking patient.

stem: Which PPE should you put on before caring for a patient coughing up blood after an assault?
options: Gloves alone
A gown alone
No PPE until blood is on you
Gloves, eyewear and a mask
explanation: Blood that can be coughed or sprayed calls for protection of the eyes, nose and mouth as well as the hands. PPE is chosen before contact, from what you expect, not after an exposure.

stem: You must use an AED on a 5-year-old and have only adult pads. What should you do?
options: Skip the AED and do CPR until pediatric pads come
Cut the adult pads in half to fit the chest
Use the adult pads without letting them touch
Wait for pediatric pads to arrive before any shock
explanation: Pediatric pads or a child setting are preferred for children under 8, but adult pads are better than no shock. Place them so they do not touch, front and back if needed.

stem: When is an oral airway the right adjunct?
options: A confused patient who is talking
A patient who gags when you check the mouth
An unresponsive patient with no gag reflex
A patient with clenched teeth
explanation: An oral airway keeps the tongue from blocking the airway in a patient who cannot protect it. A gag reflex or clenched teeth mean the device can cause vomiting or injury.

stem: Which entry belongs in a patient care report?
options: Patient seemed to be faking the pain to us
Patient was rude, as usual
Patient probably drinks too much, per neighbors
Patient states pain is 8 out of 10
explanation: Patient states pain is 8 out of 10 is objective. Reports should be objective: what you saw, heard and did, and the patient's own words in quotes. Opinions and labels do not belong and can cause legal trouble.

stem: Where do you check the pulse of an unresponsive adult?
options: Carotid artery in the neck
Pedal pulse on the foot
Brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm
Radial artery at the wrist
explanation: In an unresponsive adult, check the carotid pulse, which is felt even when blood pressure is low. In an infant, use the brachial pulse inside the upper arm.

stem: A man with a long cough, night sweats and weight loss needs help. What should you wear in addition to gloves?
options: A gown and booties
A fit-tested N95 respirator
A surgical mask worn by you alone
Nothing more, as long as he coughs into his elbow
explanation: Those signs suggest tuberculosis, which spreads through the air. A fit-tested N95 or better respirator protects you; a surgical mask placed on the patient also helps limit spread.

stem: A short-of-breath adult has clearly low oxygen signs and is breathing adequately. Which device gives the most oxygen within EMR scope?
options: CPAP mask set by an EMT partner
Nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Simple face mask at 6 L/min
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min for comfort
explanation: A nonrebreather at 10 to 15 L/min delivers a high concentration of oxygen and is within EMR scope. Simple face masks and CPAP are listed at the EMT level in the national model.

stem: How do you choose the right size oral airway?
options: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe
Length of the patient's index finger
Tip of the nose to the point of the chin
Width of the patient's palm across the knuckles
explanation: Hold the airway against the face: it should reach from the corner of the mouth to the bottom of the earlobe or the angle of the jaw. Too long can push the epiglottis closed; too short can push the tongue back.

stem: Which skin finding best suggests poor perfusion?
options: Pale, cool and moist skin
Tanned skin with freckles
Pink, warm and dry skin
Red, flushed skin after hard exercise
explanation: When blood flow drops, the body pulls blood from the skin, leaving it pale, cool and clammy. Pink, warm, dry skin is normal.

stem: Why does the mechanism of injury matter during scene size-up?
options: It tells you who was at fault
It hints at hidden injuries
It sets the patient's treatment
It replaces a physical exam
explanation: A high-energy mechanism such as a rollover or a long fall warns you to look for injuries you cannot yet see. It guides your suspicion and your resource request but never replaces assessing the patient.

stem: Which naloxone routes are within EMR scope under the national model?
options: Nebulized
Intraosseous
Intravenous push through a new line
Intranasal unit dose and auto-injector
explanation: The national scope model lets EMRs give naloxone for suspected opioid overdose by unit-dosed intranasal device or auto-injector. IV and IO routes are AEMT and above.

stem: An unresponsive adult is found after a fall. On what basis can you treat him?
options: A court order from a judge
Implied consent
Informed refusal
Expressed consent
explanation: When a patient cannot give consent and needs emergency care, the law assumes a reasonable person would want treatment. This is implied consent.

stem: While you ventilate an unresponsive man, he vomits and you hear gurgling. What should you do first?
options: Raise his head on a pillow
Give faster breaths
Insert a larger oral airway
Suction the mouth
explanation: Gurgling means fluid in the upper airway. Roll him if needed and suction before you go on ventilating, or the vomit will be pushed into the lungs.

stem: How often should you reassess the vital signs of a stable patient while waiting for EMS?
options: About every 15 minutes
Every 30 seconds
Only once at the start
Only when the patient asks you to check
explanation: Reassess a stable patient about every 15 minutes and an unstable patient about every 5 minutes, and after every intervention.

stem: Direct pressure does not stop heavy bleeding from a forearm wound. Where do you place a tourniquet?
options: Directly over the wound
2 to 3 inches above the wound
Over the elbow joint
Below the wound near the hand
explanation: Place the tourniquet on bare skin 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint, and tighten it until the bleeding stops. Write down the time it went on.

stem: At a two-car crash, the driver you reach says his daughter was in the back seat. The back seat is empty. What should you do next?
options: Wait for police to search later
Assume a relative already picked her up
Search the area for the child
Treat the driver and ignore the remark
explanation: Finding every patient is part of size-up. A child may have walked away or been thrown from the car. Look nearby and tell incoming units there may be another patient.

stem: A woman with known bee allergy has hives and trouble breathing. Under the national model, what is the EMR's role with an epinephrine auto-injector?
options: No EMS level may give epinephrine
EMRs may give it only IV
EMT and above; states may add EMRs
Any EMR may always inject it
explanation: The 2019 national model lists the epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis at the EMT level and above, though some states add it for EMRs. Support the airway, call ALS early and follow your state and medical director.

stem: An adult breathes 8 times a minute with shallow chest rise and gray lips. What does she need?
options: Time to rest, then a full reassessment
Ventilations with a BVM and oxygen
A nasal cannula at 2 L/min
A nonrebreather mask with no other care
explanation: A slow rate with shallow breaths is inadequate breathing, even though she breathes on her own. She needs assisted ventilation; a mask alone gives oxygen but does not move enough air.

stem: You arrive alone to find a bus on its side with many people injured. What is your first action?
options: Call for more resources
Splint the closest open fracture
Help the walking patients leave
Begin CPR on the first patient
explanation: When patients outnumber you, call early for more units, supervisors and incident command support. One responder who stops to treat one patient cannot help the rest.

stem: A patient with a properly placed tourniquet complains that it hurts badly. What should you do?
options: Loosen it a little every few minutes
Leave it tight and explain why
Take it off and use a pressure bandage
Move it below the wound so the hand gets blood
explanation: A working tourniquet is painful. Do not loosen it to relieve pain: bleeding will restart. Reassure the patient and let the next level of care know when it was applied.

stem: A conscious driver complains of neck pain after a rollover. What is within EMR scope?
options: Strapping him to a long spine board on scene
Manual stabilization and a cervical collar
Leaving him unsupported
A seated extrication device such as a KED
explanation: The national model adds the cervical collar and manual cervical stabilization at the EMR level. Long boards and seated devices such as the KED are EMT-level tools.

stem: An alert, oriented adult with a cut hand refuses care after you explain the risks. What should you do?
options: Call police to force treatment on the patient
Treat him anyway, since he is injured and bleeding
Respect it, document it and advise calling back
Leave without a word
explanation: A competent adult may refuse care. Make sure he understands the risks, try to persuade him, document the refusal and tell him to call back if he changes his mind.

stem: An adult has a strong pulse but is not breathing. How often do you give a rescue breath?
options: Every 10 seconds
Every 6 seconds
Every 2 to 3 seconds
Every 15 seconds
explanation: An adult with a pulse who is not breathing gets 1 breath every 6 seconds, about 10 a minute, each just enough to make the chest rise. Children and infants get a breath every 2 to 3 seconds.

stem: Using SALT, you ask patients who can walk to move to a set area. What is the next global sort step?
options: Open the airway of every child you can reach
Ask the rest to wave or move a limb
Tag every walking patient as minimal before moving on
Begin CPR on anyone who is not breathing
explanation: SALT sorts first by walking, then asks those who cannot walk to wave or show purposeful movement. Those who do neither are assessed first, then those who wave, then the walkers. Tags come later in the individual assessment.

stem: How should you splint a suspected broken forearm?
options: Straighten it with force first
Include the wrist and elbow
Wrap it tightly around the fingers
Splint only the broken spot
explanation: Immobilize the joints above and below a long-bone injury so the bone ends cannot move, and check pulse, movement and sensation before and after.

stem: A woman hit by a car is anxious, pale and has a fast, weak pulse. Her blood pressure is still normal. What do you suspect?
options: Simple anxiety
A heart attack
No problem while the pressure is normal
Early shock
explanation: Restlessness, pallor and a fast pulse are early signs of shock. Blood pressure often stays normal until late, especially in young people, so do not wait for it to fall.

stem: A conscious adult at a restaurant clutches her throat and cannot speak or cough. What does current AHA guidance say to do?
options: Lay her down on the floor and give rescue breaths
Give abdominal thrusts only
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
Do a blind finger sweep
explanation: The 2025 AHA guidelines tell rescuers to alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts for a choking adult or child until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive.

stem: A woman suddenly cannot raise her right arm and her speech is slurred. Which detail is most important to find out and pass on?
options: What she ate for lunch and when she ate it
Her insurance details and doctor's name
Her childhood illnesses and old surgeries
The time she was last known well
explanation: Stroke treatments depend on how long ago symptoms began. If no one saw the onset, the time she was last known to be normal is used. Get it and pass it on.

stem: A neighbor asks what is wrong with the patient you just treated. What should you say?
options: The diagnosis, since a neighbor is like family
That you cannot share patient information
Whatever the patient's family allows
Only the patient's medicines
explanation: Patient information is private. Share it only with those involved in the patient's care or as the law requires, not with curious neighbors.

stem: You see a tanker leaking a cloud from its valve. Which actions are correct? Select two.
options: Walk closer to read the label
Look up the placard in the ERG
Treat patients in the cloud first
Stay uphill and upwind
Drive through the cloud quickly
explanation: Distance and position protect you: stay uphill and upwind and identify the product from a safe distance, using the placard number and the Emergency Response Guidebook. Entering the cloud is for trained hazmat teams with the right protection.

stem: A cook has a fresh burn on his forearm from hot oil. What should you do first?
options: Cool it with clean running water
Apply butter or oil to soothe it
Pack it in ice
Pop the blisters
explanation: Cool water stops the burning and eases pain. Ice can deepen the injury, and blisters should be left intact. Then cover the burn with a dry, clean dressing.

stem: Which blood pressure method is within EMR scope under the national model?
options: Arterial line reading from a monitor
Automated cuff only
Manual cuff and stethoscope
Pulse oximeter estimate from the finger
explanation: The national scope model lists manual blood pressure at the EMR level. Automated blood pressure devices are listed at the EMT level and above.

stem: Which findings show an adult's breathing is not adequate? Select three.
options: Speaking only 1 or 2 words at a time
Rate of 16 with even rise
Speaking in full sentences
Blue tint around the lips
Pink, dry skin
Use of neck muscles to breathe
explanation: Accessory muscle use, broken speech and cyanosis are signs of failing breathing. A rate of 16 with equal chest rise, full sentences and normal skin are signs of adequate breathing.

stem: A patient is down in a smoke-filled room and must be moved now. Put the steps in order.
options: Grab the clothing at the shoulders
Make sure you can enter safely
Move to a safe area outside
Drag the patient along the long axis
Support the head between your arms
explanation: An emergency move is only for an immediate danger. Confirm your own safety, grip the shoulders of the clothing, cradle the head, pull in a straight line along the body to limit spine movement and get clear of the hazard.

stem: During an uncomplicated delivery, which actions are right? Select two.
options: Pull the baby out by the head
Push the head back in to wait
Support the baby's head as it emerges
Dry and warm the newborn
Cut the cord before the baby is out
explanation: Guide and support the head gently, then dry, warm and stimulate the newborn. Never pull on the baby or push the head back unless a cord problem needs it under higher-level care.

stem: Which findings in the primary assessment mean the patient needs rapid transport and more help? Select two.
options: Responds only to pain
Bleeding that is hard to control
A small scraped knee
A sprained wrist
Normal breathing and speech
explanation: An altered patient and uncontrolled bleeding are priority findings. They call for early transport by EMS and advanced help, while minor injuries can wait.

stem: Which steps help responders cope after a very hard call? Select two.
options: Working extra shifts back to back
Avoiding all talk about the call
Drinking alcohol to sleep
Getting rest and regular meals
Talking with peers or a support program
explanation: Peer support, employee assistance programs, sleep and healthy routines help after a hard call. Bottling it up, alcohol and overwork make stress worse.

stem: Put the steps for mouth-to-mask ventilation of an adult in order.
options: Place the mask on the face
Let the chest fall before the next breath
Breathe in until the chest rises
Seal it with both hands
Open the airway
explanation: Position and seal the mask, open the airway while holding the seal, give each breath over about a second until the chest just rises and let it fall before the next one.

stem: For each situation, choose whether it is safe to approach now or you must wait for another agency.
rows: A patient in a deep silo
A conscious fall victim in a park
A domestic fight still going on
A car on fire with fuel leaking
A child who fell at a playground
explanation: An active fight needs police, a burning car needs fire, and a silo is a confined space with deadly gases that needs a rescue team. A fall victim in a park or at a playground can be reached safely.

stem: Put the steps of using an AED on an adult in cardiac arrest in order.
options: Turn on the AED
Stand clear while it analyzes
Attach the pads to the bare chest
Deliver the shock if advised
Resume compressions at once
explanation: Power the AED, place the pads, keep everyone clear while it checks the rhythm, shock when told to and go straight back to compressions.

stem: For each patient, choose the best place to check the pulse first.
explanation: Check the carotid in an unresponsive adult and the brachial in an infant. In a responsive adult or older child, the radial pulse at the wrist is easiest and also shows the pressure is enough to reach the wrist.

stem: A patient who breathes through a neck stoma stops breathing. How do you ventilate him?
options: Wait for a paramedic to place an advanced airway
Give breaths through the nose only
Seal a mask over his mouth and nose as usual
Seal a pediatric mask over the stoma
explanation: A patient with a stoma moves air through the opening in his neck, not the mouth. A small round mask sealed over the stoma gives effective breaths.

stem: Match each OPQRST question to the letter it belongs to.
rows: On a scale of 0 to 10, how bad is it?
What makes it better or worse?
What were you doing when it started?
Does the pain go anywhere else?
explanation: Onset asks what the patient was doing when it began, provocation what changes it, region and radiation where it is and where it spreads, and severity how bad it is.

stem: At a farm call you and your partner develop drooling, pinpoint pupils and muscle twitching after a pesticide spill. What is within EMR scope under the national model?
options: IV fluids started for the farmer
An inhaler borrowed from a bystander
Oral glucose for each person
An agency antidote auto-injector
explanation: The national scope model lets EMRs use agency-supplied auto-injector antidotes for chemical exposures. IV fluids, inhalers and oral glucose are not EMR skills. Get clear of the spill and call hazmat as well.

stem: Under the national model, is each medication within EMR scope?
explanation: EMRs may give naloxone by intranasal unit dose or auto-injector and antidote auto-injectors for chemical exposures. Aspirin, oral glucose and inhaled bronchodilators are listed at the EMT level and above.

stem: Put the steps for preparing an oxygen cylinder in order.
options: Set the flow for the device
Check the pressure gauge
Remove the seal and crack the valve briefly
Open the cylinder valve
Attach the regulator with its washer
explanation: Cracking the valve blows dust from the outlet. Then attach the regulator, open the valve, confirm there is enough pressure and set the flow the device needs.

stem: What is the chief complaint?
options: The diagnosis you suspect after your exam
The worst injury you see
The reason dispatch gave
The problem in the patient's own words
explanation: The chief complaint is why the patient called, ideally in their own words, such as I can't breathe. Record it as said, not as your guess at a diagnosis.

stem: An unresponsive patient is breathing well and has no suspected injury. Why place her in the recovery position?
options: To raise her blood pressure while she rests
To keep her from waking up too quickly
To make chest compressions easier if she arrests
To let fluids drain from the mouth
explanation: Lying on her side lets vomit and saliva drain out instead of into the airway, while you keep watching her breathing.

stem: Bystanders press around a patient and block your work. What is the best response?
options: Ask the patient to send them away
Ignore them and keep working
Give a calm, clear request to step back
Shout at them to leave the area at once
explanation: A calm, direct request usually works, and you can give a helpful bystander a task such as watching for the ambulance. If the crowd turns hostile, retreat and call police.

stem: Which handoff to the arriving EMT is most useful?
options: Complaint, findings, care and changes
The patient's address and phone number
How long you waited for them to arrive on scene
A guess at the diagnosis only
explanation: A short, organized handoff gives the next crew what they need: who the patient is, the complaint, what you found, what you did and how the patient has responded.

stem: You stop your car at a highway crash at night. Where is the safest place to park?
options: Behind the crash, angled to shield the scene
On the far shoulder across the median, facing traffic
In front of the crash with lights off
Across all lanes to stop the traffic flow
explanation: Parking behind the crash, angled with your lights on, forms a barrier that protects you and the patients from traffic. Wear a high-visibility vest and set warning devices if you have them.

stem: How deep should you compress the chest of a 6-year-old in cardiac arrest?
options: Just enough to move the skin, to protect the ribs
About one third of the chest, about 2 inches
About 1 inch
About half the depth of the chest
explanation: Children are compressed about one third the depth of the chest, roughly 2 inches, using one or two hands. Shallow compressions do not move enough blood.

stem: A man answers your questions but cannot tell you the day or where he is. How do you describe him on AVPU?
options: Alert but disoriented
Responds to pain
Responds to verbal stimulus
Unresponsive
explanation: He is awake with eyes open and talking on his own, so he is Alert on AVPU. His confusion is described separately as disorientation to time and place.

stem: In which patient is capillary refill most useful as a sign of perfusion?
options: A 3-year-old with vomiting
A 70-year-old in a cold room
An adult with cold hands outdoors
A patient wearing nail polish
explanation: Capillary refill is most reliable in young children, such as a 3-year-old. Cold temperatures, age and some medicines make it unreliable in adults.

stem: What is offline medical direction?
options: Instructions read out by the dispatcher on the radio
A nurse's advice by phone from the hospital
A doctor's orders by radio
Written protocols and standing orders
explanation: Offline medical direction is the set of written protocols, standing orders and training approved by the medical director. Online direction is real-time orders by radio or phone.

stem: You enter a house where two people have headaches and nausea and a space heater is running. You feel dizzy. What should you do?
options: Open one window and treat inside
Give oxygen to the sickest person first
Leave and get everyone outside
Turn off the heater and stay to treat them inside
explanation: Headaches and nausea in several people, with you now affected, point to carbon monoxide. Get yourself and the occupants into fresh air, and call fire to check the building. You cannot help anyone if you are overcome.

stem: Which method of infant chest compression does the 2025 AHA guidance drop?
options: Two thumbs with hands encircling the chest
Compressions with a full ratio and breaths
Two fingers on the breastbone
The heel of one hand
explanation: The 2025 guidance dropped the two-finger technique because it often fails to reach the right depth. Rescuers use two thumbs with the hands around the chest, or the heel of one hand.

stem: An unresponsive cyclist was thrown over a car hood. Which maneuver opens her airway?
options: Jaw thrust
Recovery position first
Neck roll under the shoulders
Head tilt-chin lift
explanation: With a mechanism that could injure the spine, the jaw thrust opens the airway with little neck movement. If it fails to open the airway, the airway still takes priority.

stem: After a head injury, one pupil is large and does not react to light. What should you do?
options: Keep shining a light into it until it reacts
Report it as a sign of pressure on the brain
Ignore it as a normal finding
Cover the eye with a patch
explanation: Unequal pupils after head trauma can mean pressure building inside the skull. Report it at once to the arriving EMS crew, who will need to hurry transport.

stem: Heavy bleeding comes from a deep wound in the groin where a tourniquet will not fit. What should you do?
options: Lay a thin bandage on top and watch closely
Pack the wound and hold firm pressure
Raise the leg and wait
Apply ice and watch it
explanation: Junctional wounds such as the groin or armpit cannot take a limb tourniquet. Packing gauze deep into the wound and holding hard pressure stops the bleeding. Wound packing is within EMR scope.

stem: What PPE do you need to take a pulse on a calm patient with intact skin and no fluids present?
options: A full face shield and gown
Gloves and a respirator
Gloves and a gown
Gloves
explanation: Gloves are the basic standard precaution for patient contact. Eye protection, gowns and respirators are added when splashes, heavy contamination or airborne disease are expected.

stem: You and a second rescuer give CPR to a 4-year-old. What ratio do you use?
options: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Compressions only, with no breaths at all
30 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath at any age
explanation: With two rescuers on a child or infant, use 15:2. A single rescuer uses 30:2 for every age.

stem: An unresponsive patient has clenched teeth and snoring breaths. Under the national scope model, which airway adjunct is outside EMR scope?
options: A bag-valve mask
A nasal airway
A suction catheter for the mouth
An oral airway
explanation: The national scope model lists the nasal airway at the EMT level and above. An EMR uses manual maneuvers, suction, an oral airway when there is no gag reflex, and a BVM.

stem: You realize you wrote the wrong pulse rate on a paper report. How do you fix it?
options: Black it out completely
One line through it, then the correction, initialed and dated
Tear out the page and start over on a new one
Erase it and write over it
explanation: A single line keeps the original readable and shows a correction, not a cover-up. Add the correct value with your initials and the date.

stem: How should you position a patient in shock with no suspected spine or leg injury?
options: Head down on a steep slope with legs up
Standing to help blood reach the legs
Flat on the back and kept warm
Sitting upright in a chair
explanation: Lay the patient flat and prevent heat loss with blankets. Steep head-down positions are no longer advised, and sitting up can worsen low blood flow to the brain.

stem: Dispatch sends you to an unresponsive 2-year-old found in a backyard pool. What should you plan on the way?
options: Airway and breathing support right away
Splinting both legs before any other care
A slow, detailed history from the parents first
A long, slow search of the yard for other patients
explanation: A child pulled from water needs immediate airway and breathing care, since drowning causes arrest through lack of oxygen. Ready your ventilation equipment and plan to start rescue breaths early.

stem: A patient with mild shortness of breath will not tolerate a mask. What can you use?
options: Nonrebreather at 2 L/min
Oxygen blown at the face from a tube
Nasal cannula at 1 to 6 L/min
A BVM held loosely over the face
explanation: A nasal cannula gives low to moderate oxygen at 1 to 6 L/min and is easier to tolerate. A nonrebreather needs a high flow to keep the bag full.

stem: Why should each suction attempt on an adult be kept short?
options: Suction removes oxygen too
It loosens the patient's teeth
It drains the suction battery
Long suction cools the airway
explanation: Suction pulls out air along with fluid, so long attempts cause low oxygen. Keep each attempt brief, about 15 seconds or less for an adult, and oxygenate between attempts.

stem: You find a pulse of 44 in an adult who is pale and confused. What does this mean?
options: A sign of good fitness in a healthy adult
A normal resting rate
A slow rate with poor perfusion is serious
Nothing until you check it again in 15 minutes
explanation: A rate under 60 with signs of poor perfusion such as confusion and pallor is dangerous and needs rapid transport and advanced help. A slow pulse is only reassuring in a well, alert, fit person.

stem: Which findings should prompt a request for advanced life support? Select two.
options: Chest pain with cold, clammy skin
A nosebleed that has stopped
A small cut on the hand
A sprained ankle
A seizure that will not stop
explanation: A patient who may be having a heart attack with poor perfusion, or a seizure that keeps going, may need medications and monitoring beyond the EMR level. The minor injuries can wait for routine transport.

stem: After intranasal naloxone, an overdose patient wakes, breathes well and wants to leave. What should you know?
options: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does
A second dose is never needed after waking
He is safe to drive himself home after an hour
He can no longer stop breathing
explanation: Many opioids last longer than naloxone, so breathing can slow again. Keep monitoring, encourage EMS transport and be ready to support breathing.

stem: You start care for a patient. Which act could count as abandonment?
options: Asking a paramedic who arrives to take over
Leaving before an equal or higher level takes over
Handing off to an arriving EMT
Staying with the patient until the ambulance leaves
explanation: Once you begin care, you must continue until you hand off to someone with equal or higher training. Walking away before then is abandonment.

stem: A 6-month-old is choking and cannot cry or cough. What does current AHA guidance say to do?
options: Hold the infant upside down by the ankles and shake
Do a blind finger sweep
Give abdominal thrusts
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts
explanation: For a choking infant, the 2025 AHA guidelines call for 5 back blows alternating with 5 chest thrusts using the heel of one hand. Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of injury risk.

stem: A responsive man complains only of pain in his right ankle after a slip. Which exam fits?
options: No exam at all until EMS arrives on scene
A check of his pupils and nothing else
A full head-to-toe exam before anything else
A focused exam of the ankle and leg
explanation: With a minor mechanism and one complaint in an alert patient, a focused exam of the injured area, including pulse, movement and feeling below it, is enough.

stem: A man kicked by a horse has a bruised belly, thirst and a fast, weak pulse. What is the best care?
options: Treat for shock and speed his transport
Massage the bruised area to ease the pain
Wait to see if the bruise grows before acting
Have him drink water for his thirst
explanation: These signs point to internal bleeding you cannot stop in the field. Keep him flat and warm, give oxygen, and get him to a hospital quickly. Nothing by mouth.

stem: In the SALT individual assessment, a patient who is breathing has a pulse, follows commands and has bleeding controlled, but you judge he will likely not survive with the resources at hand. Which category fits?
options: Immediate
Delayed
Expectant
Minimal
explanation: SALT places a patient who meets the immediate criteria but is unlikely to survive given current resources in the expectant category. That patient is rechecked as resources arrive.

stem: A runner is confused and hot after a race in the heat. What is the most important treatment?
options: Cool her rapidly
Give her a warm drink
Have her keep walking
Wrap her in a blanket
explanation: Confusion with a high body temperature is heat stroke, a true emergency. Move her to shade and cool her fast, ideally by immersion in cold water or with wet towels and fanning.

stem: A choking adult goes limp in your arms. What do you do after lowering him to the floor?
options: Do a blind finger sweep
Give back blows to him on the floor
Keep giving abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
Start CPR, checking the mouth before breaths
explanation: Once a choking patient becomes unresponsive, start CPR. Compressions may move the object. Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth and remove an object only if you can see it.

stem: Which lifesaving step does SALT allow during the individual assessment before you move on?
options: Bandaging minor scrapes and small cuts
Taking a full set of vitals
Controlling major bleeding
Splinting a closed fracture
explanation: SALT lets you do quick lifesaving steps such as controlling major bleeding, opening the airway and, for a child, two rescue breaths, then move on. Splints, full vitals and dressings come after triage.

stem: Which steps are correct when applying a tourniquet? Select three.
options: Note the time it was applied
Loosen it every 10 minutes
Cover it with clothing
Place it over the knee
Place it on bare skin
Tighten until bleeding stops
explanation: A tourniquet goes on bare skin above the wound, is tightened until the bleeding stops and has its time recorded where everyone can see it. It must stay visible and must not be loosened.

stem: A man pulled from snow is cold and drowsy but breathing. What should you do?
options: Have him walk around to warm up his legs
Give him an alcoholic drink to warm his core
Rub his arms and legs hard to warm them
Handle him gently and warm him
explanation: A very cold heart is irritable, so rough handling can trigger a dangerous rhythm. Move him gently, remove wet clothing, insulate him and warm the trunk.

stem: A 10-year-old was hurt at soccer and no parent can be reached. She needs care now. What applies?
options: No care until a parent agrees
Implied consent for emergency care
Her coach must sign for her
Only the child's own consent
explanation: Minors usually need a parent's consent, but when a child needs emergency care and no parent can be reached, implied consent allows treatment. Keep trying to reach the parent.

stem: While you ventilate a child with a BVM, her belly swells. What should you change?
options: Squeeze the bag harder so more air goes in
Breathe faster to keep up with her rate
Press on the belly to empty it
Give slower, smaller breaths
explanation: Air going into the stomach means breaths are too big or too fast. Smaller, slower breaths that just make the chest rise reduce distension; pressing on the belly can cause vomiting.

stem: While you assess a patient, a family member grows angry and picks up a kitchen knife. What should you do?
options: Ask him to put the knife away in a kitchen drawer
Leave with your partner and call police
Take the knife away
Keep treating and ignore him
explanation: When a scene becomes unsafe, your first duty is your own safety. Back away, leave by a route you know, and call police. Do not try to disarm anyone.

stem: Under the national model, which statements about an EMR and ambulance transport are true? Select two.
options: An EMT or higher must be in the patient compartment
An EMR may be the only attendant
An EMR may not touch the patient en route
An EMR may assist with care in the ambulance
An EMR must drive with lights on
explanation: The national model says an EMR may help with care during transport, but an EMT or higher must be in the patient compartment and responsible for care.

stem: Put the parts of the primary assessment of a responsive trauma patient in order.
options: Control major bleeding
Check responsiveness
Decide on transport priority
Form a general impression
Check the airway and breathing
explanation: After the first look and a check of responsiveness, life-threatening bleeding is handled at once, then airway and breathing, and the findings set how urgent the patient is.

stem: Which signs point to a severe airway obstruction? Select two.
options: No sound when trying to speak
Normal breathing between coughs
Forceful coughing
A weak, silent cough
Clear, loud speech
explanation: A person who cannot speak or has a weak, silent cough is not moving enough air and needs help now. Forceful coughing and clear speech mean the airway is partly open, so encourage coughing and watch closely.

stem: Which findings should make you think of a stroke? Select two.
options: Sudden trouble speaking
One side of the face droops
A cut on the forehead
A cough with a fever
Pain in both knees for weeks
explanation: A face droop and sudden speech trouble are classic stroke signs, along with one-sided arm weakness, balance and vision changes. The other findings point elsewhere.

stem: Match each role to its job under the Incident Command System.
rows: Sets objectives for the whole incident
explanation: The incident commander leads and sets objectives, triage sorts patients, logistics finds supplies and equipment, and the public information officer speaks to the media.

stem: Put the parts of a scene size-up in order as you arrive.
options: Request more resources if needed
Count the patients
Check the scene for hazards
Note the mechanism or nature of illness
Put on the PPE you need
explanation: You look for danger before you get out, choose PPE before contact, work out what happened, find every patient and then call for the help the scene needs.

stem: Put the steps of placing a cervical collar on a seated patient in order.
options: Size the collar
Check movement and feeling in the hands
Slide the back of the collar behind the neck
Hold the head still in line
Fasten the front and recheck
explanation: Manual stabilization comes first and continues throughout. Check function, measure and size the collar, place it and fasten it, then recheck movement and feeling.

stem: Why take a set of baseline vital signs early?
options: To replace the history
To decide whether to wear gloves or not
To make a diagnosis
To compare with later sets
explanation: Baseline vitals give you a starting point. Repeated sets show whether the patient is getting better or worse, which matters more than any single number.

stem: Under the national scope model, is each airway skill within EMR scope?
explanation: The national model gives EMRs the oral airway, upper airway suction and all the mouth-to-barrier methods, including through a stoma. Supraglottic airways are AEMT and above, and CPAP is EMT and above.

stem: For each patient, choose the protection you need beyond gloves.
rows: A clean cut on the arm
explanation: Measles and tuberculosis spread through the air and need a fit-tested respirator. Vomit can splash into the eyes, so add eye protection. A clean cut or a faint with no fluids needs gloves only.

stem: Under the national model, is each device or skill within EMR scope?
explanation: EMRs may stabilize an injured limb by hand, splint it and place a cervical collar. Traction splints and long spine boards are listed at the EMT level and above.

stem: For each patient, choose whether care is a high priority or can wait.
rows: Fast, weak pulse with pale skin
Trouble breathing with a pale face
Calm and alert with a small bruise
explanation: Signs of shock, an unresponsive patient and breathing trouble are priority findings. A painful finger or a small bruise in an alert patient can wait.

stem: After a call you used the last two pairs of gloves in your kit. What should you do?
options: Borrow from the ambulance later
Use bare hands on the next call
Wait until the weekly equipment check
Restock before the next call
explanation: Restock right after a call so the next patient does not meet an empty kit. Ensuring enough supplies is part of an EMR's job.

stem: How long should you look, listen and feel for breathing in an unresponsive adult before acting?
options: Until a second responder arrives
About 30 seconds
No more than 10 seconds
A full minute of watching and listening
explanation: Check breathing, and the pulse at the same time if you are trained to, for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing and calls for CPR.

stem: A swimmer is struggling 20 feet from a dock. You are not trained in water rescue. What should you do?
options: Throw a floating object and call for help
Wade out
Wait on shore without acting
Swim out to tow her back to the dock
explanation: Reach or throw, do not go: an untrained rescuer who swims out often drowns too. A ring, cooler or rope gives the swimmer something to hold while trained rescuers come.

stem: A worker splashed a cleaning chemical in her eye. What should you do?
options: Put drops of milk in it
Rub it with a dry cloth
Flush it with water for a long time
Cover it and wait for EMS
explanation: Flush the eye right away with plenty of clean water, away from the other eye, and keep going until EMS takes over. Eye irrigation is within EMR scope.

stem: A conscious patient has a heavy nosebleed. How should she sit?
options: Leaning forward while pinching the nose
Lying on her stomach
Leaning back with the head tilted toward the ceiling
Lying flat on her back with her head turned
explanation: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat, where it can be swallowed or inhaled, and firm pinching of the soft part of the nose slows the bleeding.

stem: An alert patient breathing adequately is mildly short of breath. Your protocol calls for low-flow oxygen. Which device fits?
options: Mouth-to-mask breaths
Bag-valve mask
Oral airway
Nasal cannula
explanation: A patient who is breathing adequately needs oxygen, not ventilation. A nasal cannula gives low-flow oxygen and is within EMR scope. A BVM and rescue breaths are for inadequate breathing.

stem: Put the regions of a full-body exam of a trauma patient in order.
options: Abdomen
Head
Pelvis
Chest
Neck
Legs and arms
explanation: A head-to-toe exam runs in order so nothing is missed: head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, then the extremities, with the back checked when the patient is rolled.

stem: A motorcycle rider lies in the road on a blind curve and traffic is still moving. What should happen first?
options: Protect the scene from traffic
Drag him onto the shoulder
Remove his helmet right away
Start a head-to-toe exam
explanation: Approaching cars are the main hazard. Use your vehicle, lights and warning devices or have police stop traffic before you kneel in the road. Move him only if he is in immediate danger.

stem: An 82-year-old fell at home and seems slightly confused. Her family says this is new. What should you think?
options: Confusion is normal at her age
She is likely only tired
No care is needed if she can stand
New confusion may signal a serious problem
explanation: A sudden change in mental status in an older adult is never just age. It can mean a head injury, low oxygen, infection or stroke. Report the change and its timing to EMS.

stem: While treating a child, you notice bruises of different ages and an unlikely story. What should you do?
options: Accuse the parents on scene and leave with the child
Ask the child to keep it a secret from the parents
Ignore it, since you are not a police officer
Report your concern as your state requires
explanation: Signs of possible abuse must be reported to the proper authority as state law requires. Stay professional with the family, document what you saw and heard, and pass your concern on at handoff.

stem: A worker has a metal rod stuck in his thigh with little bleeding. What should you do?
options: Pull it out and press on the wound
Twist it to check how deep it goes
Stabilize it in place with bulky dressings
Cut it flush with the skin yourself
explanation: Leave an impaled object in place, since it may be plugging a bleeding vessel. Pad around it to keep it from moving and control bleeding around it. Removal happens at the hospital, except an object blocking the airway or CPR.

stem: Which signs show an infant is working too hard to breathe? Select three.
options: Grunting at the end of each breath
Nostrils flaring with each breath
Sleeping calmly
Pink lips and quiet breathing
Feeding well from a bottle
Skin pulling in between the ribs
explanation: Nasal flaring, retractions between the ribs and grunting are signs of respiratory distress in an infant. Pink lips, quiet breathing, good feeding and calm sleep are reassuring.

stem: Who may receive an agency-supplied antidote auto-injector from an EMR at a chemical exposure under the national model?
options: Only the EMR's own partner on the call
Only patients older than 65
Exposed people, per protocol
No one, unless an EMT is standing beside the EMR
explanation: The scope model lists auto-injector antidotes for chemical and hazardous material exposures at every level from EMR up, given to exposed people under medical direction and protocol.

stem: Under the national model, after giving intranasal naloxone to a patient who is still not breathing, what must you keep doing?
options: Sit him up and slap his face
Give him a cold shower to wake him up
Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
Wait quietly for the drug to work
explanation: Naloxone takes minutes to work and may not be enough. Keep ventilating until breathing returns and start CPR if he has no pulse. A shower or slaps waste time.

stem: Why must you let the chest come all the way back up after each compression?
options: It lets the patient take a breath on his own
It rests your arms
The heart refills with blood
It keeps the ribs from cracking
explanation: Full chest recoil lets blood flow back into the heart before the next push. Leaning on the chest cuts blood flow.

stem: You arrive at a crash where a pickup lies on its side and rocks slightly. What should you do before reaching the driver?
options: Push it back onto its wheels
Have it stabilized first
Break the windshield to reach in
Climb onto it to open a door
explanation: An unstable vehicle can roll onto you or the patient. Wait for fire or rescue to crib and stabilize it before you enter or reach inside.

stem: When does an EMR have a duty to act?
options: While on duty and called to respond
Only with a doctor present
Only when paid by the patient
Whenever they see any accident, on or off duty
explanation: On duty, an EMR has a legal duty to respond and give care. Off duty, rules vary by state, and Good Samaritan laws may protect people who help in good faith.

stem: During a trauma exam, what does the T in DCAP-BTLS stand for?
options: Tenderness
Temperature
Tremor
Tourniquet time
explanation: DCAP-BTLS stands for deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures or penetrations, burns, tenderness, lacerations and swelling.

stem: Why is the airway checked before almost everything else?
options: It takes the least time
It is the easiest step to do
Without it, oxygen cannot reach the lungs
It tells you the patient's history and medicines
explanation: Every other treatment fails if air cannot reach the lungs. A blocked airway can kill within minutes, so it comes first in the primary assessment along with major bleeding.

stem: Which resting pulse is within the normal range for an adult?
options: 40 a minute
72 a minute
130 a minute
150 a minute
explanation: A normal adult resting pulse is about 60 to 100, so 72 is normal. Children and infants have faster normal rates.

stem: How long should pauses in chest compressions last?
options: As long as the AED needs
Under 10 seconds
About 20 seconds each time
About 30 seconds
explanation: Keep pauses for breaths, rhythm checks or shocks under 10 seconds. Blood flow stops the moment compressions stop.

stem: When should you clean your hands during a call?
options: Only if you touched blood or vomit directly
Only when they look dirty
Before and after patient contact
After gloves come off
explanation: Clean your hands before you touch a patient and after contact, including after taking off gloves. Gloves can have tiny holes, and hands pick up germs from the gloves as they come off.

stem: What defines what an EMR may do on a call?
options: Anything learned from a training video online
Whatever the patient asks for
Whatever a bystander on scene suggests
State law, medical direction and protocols
explanation: Each state sets the legal scope of practice, using the national model as a guide, and the medical director sets local protocols. Act only within both.

stem: Why ask which medicines a patient takes?
options: To decide whether to wear gloves
They hint at the patient's illnesses
To check the patient's insurance before transport
So you can give the patient a dose of each one
explanation: A list of medicines tells you about conditions the patient may not mention, such as heart failure or diabetes. EMRs do not give the patient's own prescriptions.

stem: Two rescuers are doing CPR. How often should they switch who compresses?
options: Only when one rescuer is fully exhausted
Never during the call
Every 10 minutes
About every 2 minutes
explanation: Compression quality drops as rescuers tire, often before they notice. Swap about every 2 minutes, at the AED analysis, with a quick change.

stem: An unresponsive man takes a slow gasp every 10 seconds. How should you treat this?
options: As a sign he is waking up
As a reason to wait and watch him
As adequate breathing for now
As no normal breathing
explanation: Occasional gasps, called agonal breaths, are a sign of cardiac arrest, not real breathing. If he has no pulse, start CPR.

stem: Which sign of shock in a child tends to appear last?
options: A falling blood pressure
A fast heart rate that keeps climbing
Slow capillary refill in the fingertips
Cool hands and feet with mottled skin
explanation: Children hold their blood pressure up until they are near collapse. A fast pulse, cool skin and slow refill come first; low blood pressure is a late and ominous sign.

stem: A patient in arrest has a hairy, wet chest. What should you do before placing AED pads?
options: Dry the chest and remove hair if needed
Place the pads over a shirt
Rub lotion on the skin so the pads slide
Place the pads on the belly, below the wet skin
explanation: Pads need full skin contact. Wipe the chest dry and shave or pull away hair under the pads, using a spare set if needed.

stem: Why do you peel the first glove off inside out and hold it in the other gloved hand?
options: To check the gloves for tears after use
To keep the outside from touching skin
To make the used gloves easier to recycle
To save the gloves for reuse
explanation: Turning the gloves inside out traps the contaminated outer surface inside. Your bare skin then touches only the clean inner side of the second glove.

stem: A used needle sticks your hand during a call. What should you do?
options: Cover it and report it at next month's meeting
Keep it quiet to avoid the extra paperwork
Wait to see if you feel sick
Wash the site and report it at once
explanation: Wash the area with soap and water and report the exposure right away so testing and preventive treatment can start in time.

stem: A diabetic man is sweaty, shaky and confused. Under the national scope model, what can an EMR do?
options: Give him oral glucose gel between cheek and gum
Check his blood sugar with his own meter
Inject his own insulin
Protect his airway and call for EMS
explanation: Blood glucose checks and oral glucose are EMT-level skills in the national model. An EMR keeps him safe, protects the airway, gathers the history and gets EMS on the way. State protocols may add more.

stem: You see a bulge under the skin below an arrest patient's collarbone. How should you place the AED pad?
options: Directly over the bulge
Away from the bulge
Skip the AED entirely
On the arm instead
explanation: The bulge is likely a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator. Place the pad so it is not directly over the device and use the AED as usual.

stem: A patient's blood splashes into your eye. What should you do first?
options: Wait until the call ends, then rinse it
Flush the eye with plenty of water
Cover the eye with gauze until the call ends
Rub the eye gently to clear the blood out
explanation: Flush the eye at once with water or saline, then report the exposure to your supervisor so you can be evaluated quickly. Rubbing can push material deeper.

stem: In an adult, how is an oral airway usually inserted?
options: Tip toward the roof of the mouth, then rotated
Tip pointing toward the tongue and pushed straight in
Through one nostril
Sideways along the cheek and left there
explanation: In adults the airway goes in with the tip pointing to the roof of the mouth and is turned 180 degrees as it nears the back of the throat, so it rides over the tongue. In children it is often inserted with a tongue blade in its normal position.

stem: Blood soaks through the gauze you are holding on a leg wound. What should you do?
options: Rinse the wound with water
Add more gauze and press harder
Remove the gauze and start over
Lift the gauze to look
explanation: Lifting or removing soaked gauze pulls away clots. Add gauze on top and press harder; if bleeding still will not stop on a limb, apply a tourniquet.

stem: Where should a used sharp go?
options: Back into its cap by hand
Into a puncture-resistant sharps container
Into your pocket for later
Into a regular trash bag
explanation: Put used sharps straight into a puncture-resistant container. Recapping by hand is a common cause of needlesticks.

stem: Which practice is safe around oxygen?
options: Keep it away from open flames
Let a patient smoke with a cannula on
Store cylinders lying loose in a vehicle
Grease the regulator threads
explanation: Oxygen feeds fire. Keep flames and sparks away, secure cylinders and never put oil or grease on the fittings.

stem: You placed a splint on a forearm. What must you recheck after it is on?
options: Pulse, movement and feeling in the hand
The patient's blood type
The patient's pupils only
Lung sounds on both sides of the chest
explanation: A splint can press on vessels and nerves. Check circulation, movement and sensation below the injury before and after splinting.

stem: Which marking on a truck tells you it carries hazardous material you can look up?
options: A speed limiter sticker
A license plate from another state or country
A company logo painted on the driver door
A diamond placard with a four-digit number
explanation: Diamond placards show the hazard class, and the four-digit identification number can be looked up in the Emergency Response Guidebook from a safe distance.

stem: A BVM mask is soiled with saliva after a call. What should happen to it?
options: Wipe it on your sleeve and reuse it
Rinse it with tap water only
Follow your agency's cleaning rules
Leave it in the kit as is
explanation: Follow your agency's rules for single-use items and for cleaning and disinfecting reusable gear. Wear gloves while cleaning.

stem: A woman 8 months pregnant feels faint lying flat on her back. How should you position her?
options: Flat on her back
With her legs raised high on pillows
On her left side
Face down
explanation: In late pregnancy the uterus can press on the large vein that returns blood to the heart when she lies flat. Turning her onto her left side relieves it.

stem: Why is a two-person BVM technique preferred when two responders are present?
options: It lets breaths be twice as large
It doubles the oxygen flow from the tank
It avoids the need to open the airway
One holds a better mask seal
explanation: One rescuer uses both hands to hold the mask seal and keep the airway open while the other squeezes the bag. A poor seal is the most common reason BVM breaths fail.

stem: When taking a manual blood pressure, what is the systolic reading?
options: The highest number you pumped to
The first tapping sound you hear
The average of the two numbers
The point the sounds stop
explanation: As the cuff slowly deflates, the first clear tapping sound marks the systolic pressure. The point where the sounds disappear is the diastolic pressure.

stem: A patient says she is allergic to latex. What should you do?
options: Note it only if she reacts
Skip gloves altogether
Use latex-free gloves and report the allergy
Use any gloves, since contact will be brief
explanation: Latex can trigger a serious reaction in an allergic person. Switch to non-latex equipment and pass the allergy on at handoff.

stem: Right after birth, a newborn is limp and not crying. What should you do first?
options: Slap the baby's feet hard until it cries
Hold the baby upside down by the feet
Dry, warm and rub the baby
Wait 5 minutes to see if it cries
explanation: Drying and rubbing the back keeps the baby warm and often starts breathing. If the baby still does not breathe well, start ventilations with a BVM sized for a newborn.

stem: During the SALT global sort, a man lies still and does not respond to your commands. What happens next?
options: He is moved to the walkers
He is skipped until the end
He is tagged dead at once
He is assessed first
explanation: Patients who neither walk nor wave are assessed first because they are most likely to need lifesaving care. A tag is given only after the individual assessment.

stem: Which radio message is best when calling for an ambulance?
options: Brief, clear facts in plain language
Every detail of the history
Jokes to calm the crew
Codes only you understand
explanation: Keep radio traffic short and clear: location, number of patients, their condition and what you need. Plain language avoids confusion between agencies.

stem: During a delivery, a loop of umbilical cord comes out before the baby. Under the national model, what is your role?
options: Cut the cord at once
Pull the baby out quickly by the shoulders
Call for higher-level help
Push the cord back in yourself
explanation: Assisted complicated delivery is listed at the EMT level and above in the national model. Get the highest level of care coming now and help them; a prolapsed cord needs urgent hospital care.

stem: Why might a folded towel go under a small child's shoulders when you open the airway?
options: It lowers the risk of vomiting during ventilation
It stops the child from moving or rolling
It keeps the child warm on a cold floor
The large head bends the neck forward
explanation: A young child's large head flexes the neck when lying flat, which can kink the airway. A little padding under the shoulders brings the head to a neutral position.

stem: In a noisy place you cannot hear the pulse sounds. How can you estimate systolic pressure?
options: By guessing from skin color
By counting breaths
By feeling for the radial pulse to return
By pressing on a fingernail and counting the refill
explanation: Inflate the cuff until the radial pulse disappears, then let it down slowly. The reading when the pulse returns is the palpated systolic pressure. Record it as palpated.

stem: A man is found at the bottom of a staircase. Why ask what happened before he fell?
options: It shows whether he needs a cervical collar
A medical problem may have caused the fall
It tells you who is to blame
It replaces the need for a trauma exam
explanation: A fall may follow a faint, seizure or heart rhythm problem. Asking about events leading up helps you treat both the cause and the injury.

stem: In SALT, a child is not breathing after you open the airway. What should you do?
options: Move on without any action
Give two rescue breaths
Tag the child dead at once
Start full CPR and stay
explanation: SALT allows two rescue breaths for a child who is not breathing after the airway is opened, since a child's arrest often starts with breathing. If breathing does not start, the child is tagged dead and you move on.

stem: Which use of patient information is allowed under HIPAA?
options: Telling friends about the call
Describing the patient to the press at the scene
Posting a photo of the scene online without names
Sharing findings with the receiving hospital
explanation: Sharing information with others caring for the patient is permitted. Posting scene photos or telling friends or the media is not.

stem: A bone end is poking through the skin of the shin. How should you handle the wound?
options: Cover it with a sterile dressing and splint
Leave it open to the air
Push the bone back under the skin, then bandage
Rinse the bone with soap
explanation: Cover an open fracture with a sterile dressing to limit contamination, control bleeding without pressing on the bone, and splint it as it lies.

stem: A man's shoulder looks out of place after a fall. What should you do?
options: Pull the arm to put it back
Have him move it in circles
Splint it in the position found
Wrap the hand to the chest very tightly
explanation: Splint a suspected dislocation as found, using a sling and padding for comfort. Putting it back can damage nerves and vessels and is not an EMR skill.

stem: You reach a house fire before fire crews. Which actions are right? Select two.
options: Enter to search bedrooms
Report people still inside
Open doors to let smoke out
Climb a ladder to a window
Stay outside the building
explanation: Without turnout gear and breathing apparatus, stay out, keep bystanders back and give arriving crews what you know about people inside. Opening doors can feed the fire.

stem: A patient who refuses care is slurring his words and smells of alcohol. What should you consider?
options: His refusal is always valid if he signs the form
You must leave at once without a signature
You can restrain him yourself until he agrees
He may not be able to refuse safely
explanation: A valid refusal needs a patient who understands the risks. Intoxication, head injury or low blood sugar can impair that. Get medical direction and police help as your protocols say.

stem: During your exam you notice a patient's breathing sounds wet and gurgling from the throat. What does this tell you?
options: There is fluid in the upper airway
The patient is asleep and resting comfortably
The patient has a fever and a chest infection
The lungs are clear
explanation: Gurgling from the throat means fluid in the upper airway that needs suction. Snoring suggests the tongue is partly blocking the airway.

stem: Which breathing rate is normal for a resting adult?
options: 6 a minute
16 a minute
32 a minute
40 a minute
explanation: A resting adult normally breathes about 12 to 20 times a minute, so 16 is normal. Rates well below or above that range, along with poor chest rise, suggest inadequate breathing.

stem: What does a thready pulse mean?
options: It skips every third beat in a regular pattern
It is weak and hard to feel
It is strong and bounding
It is slower than normal for the age
explanation: A thready pulse is weak and faint, often fast, and is a common sign of shock. A bounding pulse is unusually strong.

stem: A man is having a seizure on the floor. What should you do?
options: Hold his arms and legs still
Put something between his teeth
Pour water in his mouth
Move things away and protect his head
explanation: Protect him from injury and do not restrain him or put anything in his mouth. When the jerking stops, roll him onto his side and check breathing.

stem: Why is it useful to know the patient's age and complaint from dispatch?
options: It lets you prepare equipment
It confirms the diagnosis
It tells you the patient's full medical history
It allows you to skip the scene size-up
explanation: Dispatch details help you plan, such as readying a pediatric mask or the AED. They can be wrong, so you still size up the scene and assess the patient.

stem: Which is a warning sign of growing stress in a responder?
options: Normal interest in hobbies and family
Trouble sleeping and irritability
Steady appetite and sleep
Enjoying time off with friends and family
explanation: Sleep problems, irritability, withdrawal and loss of interest can signal stress building up. Seek support early.

stem: A patient is too confused to answer. Where can you find history?
options: Only from the patient later, once he is less confused
From guessing his age
Family, bystanders and medical ID jewelry
From the registration papers in his car
explanation: Family, bystanders, medication bottles and medical ID jewelry can give history when the patient cannot. Note the source in your report.

stem: An agitated patient is pacing and shouting but not violent. What is the best approach?
options: Speak calmly and keep a clear exit
Argue with him until he calms down and sits
Restrain him at once with a sheet and tape
Stand between him and the door to keep him in
explanation: Stay calm, use a quiet voice, keep a safe distance and never block your own way out. Mechanical restraint is not in the EMR scope; call police if he becomes violent.

stem: Which make rescue breaths more effective? Select two.
options: Skipping the airway opening
Breaths as fast as possible
Blowing until the cheeks puff
Each breath over about 1 second
Just enough air to see the chest rise
explanation: Steady one-second breaths that just raise the chest give oxygen without filling the stomach. Fast or forceful breaths push air into the stomach and can cause vomiting.

stem: Which signs fit a patient in shock? Select three.
options: Warm, pink skin
Fast, weak pulse
Slow, deep breathing
Restlessness or anxiety
Pale, sweaty skin
Strong, slow pulse
explanation: Shock makes the brain uneasy, speeds the pulse while weakening it, and pulls blood from the skin. Warm pink skin and a strong slow pulse are not typical of early shock.

stem: A hiker was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake. What is the right care?
options: Put a tourniquet above the bite
Pack the leg in ice
Cut the bite and suck out venom
Keep him calm and the leg still
explanation: Keep the patient still and calm, remove rings or tight items, splint the limb loosely and get him to a hospital. Cutting, suction, ice and tourniquets cause harm.

stem: A worker has collapsed at the bottom of a sewer access hole. What should you do?
options: Climb down quickly to check his pulse
Stay out and call a rescue team
Lower a rope and pull him up
Send a coworker down a ladder to help
explanation: Confined spaces may lack oxygen or hold toxic gas, which is why the worker collapsed. Would-be rescuers often die there. Only trained teams with air supplies should enter.

stem: What should a patient care report include? Select three.
options: Your opinion of the family
Your guess at blame for the crash
The care you gave and the response
Vital signs and findings
Times of key events and care
Rumors from bystanders
explanation: A good report records times, findings, vital signs, the care given and how the patient responded. Opinions, rumors and blame do not belong.

stem: A man has sudden weakness on one side. Which facts should you gather for the EMS crew? Select two.
options: The color of his car
Who saw the symptoms start
Where he went to school
His favorite food
When he was last known well
explanation: Last known well and the person who saw the onset help the hospital decide on time-sensitive treatment. Bring or name the witness if you can.

stem: Which actions improve survival in adult cardiac arrest? Select two.
options: Checking the pulse for a full minute
Starting compressions quickly
Using an AED as soon as it arrives
Pausing compressions to find a vein
Giving breaths before every compression
explanation: Early, high-quality compressions and early defibrillation are what most improve survival. Long pulse checks and other pauses take blood flow away.

stem: For each situation, choose the resource to request.
rows: A long ground trip for a critical patient
A gas smell in a building
A car door jammed around a trapped driver
explanation: Extrication and gas leaks need fire or rescue, threats need law enforcement, and air medical can shorten a long trip for a critical patient where local protocol allows.

stem: A choking woman is visibly pregnant. Where do you give thrusts?
options: On the upper belly
On the chest
Only on the back
On the lower belly
explanation: In late pregnancy, and for people too large to encircle, chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts so the uterus is not compressed.

stem: How can you form a quick first impression of a young child before you touch her?
options: Check her temperature under the arm
Watch her look, breathing and color
Take a blood pressure with a small cuff
Ask the parent for her full medical history
explanation: Watching from the doorway shows how the child looks and acts, how hard she works to breathe and the color of her skin. A child who is upset by touch may look worse once handled.

stem: Put the first actions of the first unit at a large incident in order.
options: Request more resources
Establish command
Begin triage
Size up the scene
explanation: The first unit sizes up the scene, takes command, calls for what is needed and then starts triage so care reaches the right patients first.

stem: Choose the usual flow range for each device.
explanation: A nasal cannula runs at 1 to 6 L/min. A nonrebreather needs 10 to 15 L/min to keep its reservoir bag inflated.

stem: Where do you start when feeling a patient's belly for pain?
options: Only on the left side, where the spleen is
Away from where it hurts
With deep, hard pressure over the whole belly
Right on the painful spot
explanation: Begin away from the painful area and move toward it last with gentle pressure, so the patient does not tense up and hide other findings.

stem: While moving a patient you find a handgun in his waistband. What should you do?
options: Unload it yourself
Stop and get law enforcement to secure it
Hide it in your kit
Leave it in place and keep moving him to the car
explanation: Weapons are a scene hazard. Do not handle the gun; tell police and let them secure it before care continues.

stem: Why should you wear a seat belt when riding in the back of an ambulance?
options: Crashes can throw unbelted riders
It speeds up the trip
It keeps the patient calm during the ride
It is only a rule for drivers, not crew
explanation: Unrestrained crew members are badly hurt in ambulance crashes. Stay belted whenever you can and secure loose equipment.

stem: How should you lift a heavy patient on a device with your partner?
options: Bend at the knees and keep your back straight
Bend at the waist and lift fast
Hold the weight far out from your body
Twist to face the door as you lift, to save time
explanation: Use your legs, keep your back straight, hold the load close and avoid twisting. Ask for more help when a patient is too heavy.

stem: A man with pinpoint pupils breathes 4 times a minute. Before giving intranasal naloxone, what should you do?
options: Wait to see if he wakes up on his own
Check his blood sugar with a meter first
Open the airway and ventilate
Sit him upright in a chair so he can breathe
explanation: Support breathing first. Breaths with a BVM or mask keep oxygen going while naloxone, which takes a few minutes to work, is prepared and given.

stem: Why is a commercial tourniquet preferred over a belt?
options: It is cheaper to replace
It reliably tightens enough to stop flow
It can be loosened every few minutes to rest the limb
It does not need to be timed or marked
explanation: Improvised tourniquets often fail to get tight enough and can just slow venous return, which makes bleeding worse. Use a commercial device when one is available.

stem: A 4-year-old has a fever and a rash. Who is often the best source of her history?
options: Her older siblings only
Her school nurse's records
A neighbor across the street
Her parent or caregiver
explanation: Caregivers know a young child's baseline, recent illness and medicines best. Talk to the child too, at her level, about what hurts.

stem: A finger was cut off in a saw accident. How should you care for the part?
options: Throw it away since it cannot be saved
Wrap it in dry gauze, bag it and keep it cool
Put it straight onto ice
Soak it in water in a cup
explanation: Wrap the part in dry sterile gauze, seal it in a plastic bag and place the bag on ice or in cool water. Direct contact with ice or soaking damages the tissue.

stem: Two people who were in a spill have chemical powder on their clothes. What should happen before you treat them?
options: They wait until the hospital
You treat them in your vehicle
You brush the powder off with your hands
They are decontaminated first
explanation: Contaminated patients can expose you and everyone else. Hazmat teams decontaminate them first, often by removing clothing and rinsing, unless you have the training and gear to help.

stem: A family shows you a valid do not resuscitate order for a patient in cardiac arrest. What should you do?
options: Ask a bystander at the scene to decide for you
Follow the order and your local protocol
Start CPR anyway every time
Ignore it unless a doctor is present on scene
explanation: A valid DNR order or similar form tells you the patient's wishes. Follow it as your state and local protocols direct; if you doubt it is valid, begin care and seek medical direction.

stem: A toddler was in a car seat during a minor crash and is awake and calm. How might you limit movement?
options: Strap him upright to an adult board
Have him walk to the ambulance
Keep the child in the seat if it is intact
Take the child out and hold him
explanation: If the car seat is undamaged and the child is stable, the seat itself can limit movement with padding added. Remove the child only if the seat is damaged or care requires it.

stem: Put the first steps for an unresponsive adult found on a sidewalk in order.
options: Call for help and an AED
Check for a response
Check breathing and pulse
Make sure the scene is safe
explanation: Confirm safety, tap and shout to check for a response, get help and an AED on the way, then check breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds.

stem: A trauma patient's pulse rises from 92 to 118 over 10 minutes while his skin grows paler. What does this trend suggest?
options: He is getting worse
He is calming down
He is getting better
The first reading was wrong
explanation: A rising pulse with paler skin suggests worsening shock. Trends across repeated vitals tell you more than one set and should be reported to the next level of care.

stem: You reassess an unstable patient. How often should this be done?
options: Only once before handoff
Only if the patient complains
About every 30 minutes
About every 5 minutes
explanation: Unstable patients are reassessed about every 5 minutes because their condition can change quickly; stable patients about every 15.

stem: Following the CDC's first example sequence, put the steps for taking off PPE in order.
options: Remove the mask or respirator
Clean your hands
Remove the gloves
Remove the gown
Remove the goggles or face shield
explanation: In the CDC's first example sequence the most contaminated items come off first: gloves, then eye protection by the clean band, then the gown, then the mask or respirator by the straps, and hands are cleaned at the end.

stem: Your oxygen cylinder gauge reads very low after a call. What should you do?
options: Store it with the full cylinders for later
Replace it before the next call
Keep using it until it is empty
Mark it full to save time
explanation: Replace a low cylinder right away and mark the empty one so it is not grabbed by mistake. A cylinder that runs out mid-call puts the patient at risk.

stem: A very heavy patient must be moved from an upstairs bedroom. What is the best plan?
options: Lift him alone to save time and space
Call for more lifting help and equipment
Have him slide down the stairs on a blanket
Leave him there and treat in place until he improves
explanation: Moving a heavy patient safely takes enough people and the right equipment. Ask early for lift assistance so no one, patient or rescuer, is injured.
